The 2026 PSLE brings significant syllabus changes to both Mathematics and Science, with topics removed, reorganised, a new Primary 6 algebra topic added, and a stronger emphasis on skills over memorisation. For Mathematics, Speed has been removed entirely while Average and Ratio move to Primary 6. For Science, the standalone Cell Structure topic has been removed while skills-based assessment is strengthened. These changes affect the 2026 PSLE cohort — students currently in Primary 6. This guide is from Ancourage Academy , whose tutors track MOE syllabus changes and adapt PSLE prep programmes accordingly. As someone who has taught Primary Mathematics for over a decade — including at Ancourage Academy — I have been tracking these MOE syllabus updates closely. Here is everything parents need to know to help their children prepare effectively. Why MOE Changed the PSLE Syllabus The updated syllabus emphasises mathematical reasoning, conceptual understanding, and problem-solving skills over rote memorisation. MOE designed these changes to allow topics to be studied at the "right time" and reduce abrupt jumps in difficulty, creating a smoother learning journey from Primary 1 to 6. "The PSLE serves as a checkpoint to assess students' understanding of core concepts and skills in the Primary School curriculum." — Ministry of Education, Singapore, Committee of Supply Debate 2026 The 2021 Mathematics Syllabus now applies to all levels, with Primary 6 students from 2026 being the first cohort using this syllabus for PSLE . Similarly, the Science syllabus has been restructured to focus on scientific inquiry rather than memorising complex terminology. The 2026 PSLE written examinations are scheduled for Thursday 24 September to Wednesday 30 September 2026 , with results expected in late November. Looking further ahead, at the March 2026 Committee of Supply debate a parliamentary question raised alternatives such as portfolio-based assessments and computer-adaptive testing . Education Minister Desmond Lee responded that MOE is "not closed off to any ideas" and will consult stakeholders broadly, but noted that PSLE serves a distinct posting function subject to "more complex considerations" than school-based assessment. While no changes are confirmed for 2026 or 2027, this signals that the examination format may evolve in coming years. Ancourage Academy's Primary Mathematics and Science programmes are fully updated for the 2026 PSLE syllabus changes — book a trial class (usually $18) for a diagnostic assessment of your child's readiness under the new format. Mathematics: Topics Removed from PSLE 2026 Speed — one of the most challenging Primary 6 topics — has been completely removed from the PSLE syllabus. This is significant because Speed problems traditionally caused major difficulty for students, combining distance, time, and rate concepts in complex word problems. In our experience teaching Primary Mathematics at Ancourage Academy, Speed-related questions historically accounted for a significant share of marks lost in Paper 2. One parent shared: "My daughter struggled with Speed for months. Knowing it's removed from the 2026 PSLE is a relief, but we're now focusing that energy on mastering Ratio instead." Additionally removed: Turns and 8-point Compass: Previously in the Angles topic at Primary 4, now removed entirely Complex speed-distance-time problems: No longer tested at PSLE level For parents whose children struggled with Speed in the past, this is welcome news. However, these concepts will still appear in Secondary Mathematics , so foundational understanding remains valuable. It marks the culmination of six years of primary education and lays the groundwork for secondary school learning. However, in 2026, there are several important updates to the syllabus and examination format you need to be aware of. While it may be confusing at first, especially for parents with children from earlier batches, these changes are part of the efforts to: Strengthen conceptual understanding Reduce unnecessary overload Better prepare students for secondary education To help keep you updated, this article will outline the most important changes to the 2026 PSLE syllabus and exam format, what they mean in practice, and how they may affect your child’s preparation journey. 1. The 2026 PSLE Will Fully Reflect the Revised Primary Mathematics Syllabus One of the most significant updates to the PSLE is that the 2026 cohort will be the first to be assessed entirely under the revised Primary Mathematics syllabus. Previously, the 2021 mathematics syllabus only applied to primary 1 to 5. This year, that same syllabus will now apply to primary 6 students as well, according to a 2025 document by the Ministry of Education (MOE) outlining the new implementation. Rather than mechanical procedures alone, the revised syllabus places greater emphasis on: Supporting the development of current-day competencies Deepening students’ understanding and appreciation of the subject Promoting self-directed learning and reflection The intent is to ensure students develop a strong foundation that supports long-term learning, especially as they move on to more abstract topics in secondary school. For students, this means PSLE math questions are designed to assess understanding more holistically, rather than relying on repetitive drilling of familiar question types. 2. Several PSLE Math Topics Have Been Removed or Repositioned Another key change to note is that certain topics traditionally associated with the PSLE have been either removed or shifted to other levels. One of the biggest examples is the removal of speed from the PSLE math syllabus . Instead, this topic is now taught in secondary school, reducing content load for Primary 6 students. At the same time, topics such as averages and ratios have been repositioned to Primary 6, while pie charts and nets are introduced earlier in the primary years. These changes are meant to support the development of problem-solving skills, as students are given more time across multiple years to revisit and apply key ideas! 3. The PSLE Mathematics Exam Format Has Been Refined Beyond the syllabus itself, the PSLE exam format for Mathematics has also been modified. While the assessment still consists of two written papers, the structure and weighting have been adjusted to better align with learning objectives. According to revised formats set by the Singapore Examinations and Assessment Board (SEAB), Paper 1 now accounts for 50 per cent of the total marks and focuses on multiple-choice and short-answer questions. This is due to the slight change in the total number of questions in both papers. For reference, here is a quick comparison of the number of questions between Paper 1 in 2025 and 2026: Paper 1 2025 2026 Multiple-choice 15 18 Short-answer 15 12 While students will still need to answer 30 questions in total, the 2026 Paper 1 will have more multiple-choice questions. With fewer short-answer questions, each question now carries greater significance. Paper 2, on the other hand, will now feature fewer questions: Paper 2 2025 2026 Short-answer 5 5 Structured/Long-answer 12 10 This means success in PSLE math is not just about getting the final answer right. In 2026, students are now encouraged to also show clear thinking and logical steps in their responses. 4. Removal of Topics in the PSLE Science Syllabus The 2026 PSLE Science paper reflects updates introduced in the revised Primary Science syllabus. One of the most notable changes is the removal of certain content-heavy topics, such as Cells, from the examinable scope. This is reflected in the 2023 science syllabus , which has been implemented progressively over the past few years. Removing the topic is meant to reduce excessive memorisation and allow students to focus more on scientific reasoning and inquiry-based learning. 5. These updates are designed to reduce excessive memorisation, strengthen conceptual understanding, and encourage deeper mathematical reasoning. The revised PSLE Maths format also includes changes to topic sequencing, paper structure, and marks allocation, making it important for parents and students to understand what to expect before the examination. Why MOE Revised the PSLE Mathematics Format Singapore’s Ministry of Education (MOE) has gradually shifted the education system towards skills-based learning instead of pure drilling and memorisation. The revised Mathematics syllabus focuses more on: Problem-solving and reasoning Application of concepts in unfamiliar situations Conceptual understanding Real-world mathematical thinking The changes are intended to help students build stronger foundations before progressing to secondary school Mathematics. Rather than simply solving repetitive question types, students are now encouraged to think critically and explain their reasoning clearly. Key Changes to the PSLE Mathematics Syllabus Several topics have been removed, shifted, or reorganised across primary levels. Topic Previous Level New Level Speed Primary 6 Secondary 1 Average Primary 5 Primary 6 Ratio Primary 5 Primary 6 Pie Charts Primary 6 Primary 4 Nets of 3D Solids Primary 6 Primary 4 Time Primary 4 Primary 3 Additionally, certain concepts related to turns and the 8-point compass have been removed entirely from the syllabus. What These Topic Changes Mean The restructuring aims to create a smoother learning progression across different primary levels. Students now learn some visual and data-related topics earlier, giving them more time to build confidence before Primary 6. Meanwhile, more advanced topics such as Ratio and Average are consolidated in Primary 6, allowing students to explore them more deeply instead of learning them gradually over multiple years. One of the biggest changes is the removal of Speed from Primary Mathematics. Many students previously found Speed challenging because it required formula memorisation and multi-step application under time pressure. Moving it to Secondary 1 reduces cognitive overload for Primary 6 students. Detailed Breakdown of the 2026 PSLE Maths Format Changes The overall examination still consists of two written papers, but there are important adjustments to marks allocation and question distribution. Under the revised format, both papers are equally important. This means students must: Pay equal attention to foundational accuracy and problem-solving Strengthen both speed and reasoning skills Avoid careless mistakes in Paper 1 Build confidence in higher-order questions in Paper 2 The increased marks in Paper 1 also mean that basic concepts and accurate working become even more important.
